items.prompt: Define inflation.
items.canonical_answer: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of an economy over a period, usually a year, so that a unit of money buys fewer goods and services than before.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must be stated exactly - what the term is, and what it covers.

items.prompt: At a Katutura market stall, the price of a loaf of bread rises from N$10 to N$12 in one month. A learner says the economy therefore has inflation. Identify the features of inflation that a rise in one good's price does not show.
items.canonical_answer: Inflation is a rise in the general price level, the cost of the whole basket a typical household buys, not the price of one good. It is sustained over a period, not one month's change, and other prices may hold or fall while bread rises.
marking_guidance: Features: what it includes - each characteristic named and separated; a definition restated is not a features answer.

items.prompt: Define the Consumer Prices Index (CPI).
items.canonical_answer: The Consumer Prices Index measures the general price level by tracking the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by a typical household, with each item weighted by its share of household spending.

items.prompt: The Consumer Prices Index of an economy stood at 120.0 last year and 126.0 this year. Calculate the economy's yearly rate of inflation.
items.canonical_answer: Inflation rate = (CPI this year - CPI last year) / CPI last year x 100. Here 126.0 - 120.0 = 6.0 index points, 6.0 / 120.0 = 0.05, and 0.05 x 100 = 5, so the rate of inflation is 5% a year.
marking_guidance: Formula: the yearly inflation rate formula must be stated or used.
Substitution: the working shows the figures put into the formula, step by step.
Answer with units: the final figure carries its unit, per cent.

items.prompt: In one year an economy's Consumer Prices Index rose by 5%. Within the basket, food prices rose 12%, bus fares rose 6%, clothing rose 2% and electronics fell 3%. Explain what the data shows about the general price level and the prices of individual goods.
items.canonical_answer: The general price level rose 5%, but the items inside it moved differently. Food rose 12% and bus fares 6%, while clothing rose 2% and electronics fell 3%. The CPI is an average weighted by spending shares, so it hides this spread: a household spending a large share of its income on food faces a rise in its cost of living well above 5%. However, a good can fall in price in a year when prices in general rise, so the 5% describes no single item.
marking_guidance: What the data shows: the relationship between the figures must be stated before anything else.
Supporting evidence: a comparison of two or more items in the data, with their figures.
Exception: an answer that notes where the pattern does not hold earns the however mark.

items.prompt: A retiree in Windhoek lives on a pension fixed at N$120 000 a year. The Consumer Prices Index rises from 120.0 to 126.0 while the pension is unchanged. Using the figures, explain what happens to the quantity of goods the pension buys.
items.canonical_answer: Prices rose by 126.0 / 120.0 = 1.05, which is 5%. The pension stays at N$120 000, so measured in last year's prices it is worth N$120 000 / 1.05 = N$114 286, about N$5 714 less. Because each dollar now buys fewer goods, the retiree must cut some purchases. Therefore the real value of the pension, the quantity of goods it buys, has fallen by about 5% even though its money value is unchanged.

items.prompt: Define demand-pull inflation.
items.canonical_answer: Demand-pull inflation is a rise in the general price level caused by total spending in the economy growing faster than its capacity to produce, so buyers compete for scarce goods and sellers raise prices.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must be stated exactly - what the term is, and what it covers.

items.prompt: In one year, total spending in an economy grows by 8% while its capacity to produce grows by 2%. Analyse how demand-pull inflation is likely to develop, and who gains and who loses as it does.
items.canonical_answer: Total spending grows 8% while capacity grows 2%, so buyers want more than firms can supply. Because buyers compete for the scarce goods, sellers can raise prices without losing sales, as lodges do when Etosha rooms run short in a busy season, and the general price level rises as shortages spread through the basket. Part of the extra spending therefore becomes higher prices rather than more output, and if workers then win higher wages to keep up, the rise can feed itself. Sellers of scarce goods gain, while savers holding money, households on fixed incomes and workers whose pay lags behind prices lose buying power.

items.prompt: The price of diesel rises from N$20 to N$25 a litre, and haulage firms pass the rise on to the shops they supply. Using the figures, explain how this is likely to lead to cost-push inflation in the economy.
items.canonical_answer: Diesel rises by N$25 - N$20 = N$5 a litre, and N$5 / N$20 = 0.25, a 25% rise. Haulage firms' costs rise and they pass this on, so moving food and stock to shops costs more and shops raise their prices. Prices rise because costs rose first, with total spending unchanged, so this is cost-push inflation. Therefore, as many goods travel by road, the fuel rise is likely to lift the general price level, not just one price.

items.prompt: Define the real value of a sum of money.
items.canonical_answer: The real value of a sum of money is the quantity of goods and services it will buy. When the general price level rises, the same sum buys fewer goods, so its real value falls; when the price level falls, its real value rises.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must be stated exactly - what the term is, and what it covers.

items.prompt: The general price level of an economy begins to fall by 2% a year, and households start to expect further falls. Analyse how this is likely to affect spending, output, jobs and a household repaying a N$50 000 loan.
items.canonical_answer: With prices falling 2% a year and expected to keep falling, buyers postpone purchases they can put off, such as furniture or a new phone. Firms' sales fall, so they cut prices further, cut output and lay off workers. Workers who lose income spend less, so prices fall again and the fall can feed itself. Meanwhile the household's N$50 000 loan stays fixed in money while each dollar buys more, so repaying it means giving up more goods, and the household cuts its spending further. Consumers who keep their jobs gain cheaper goods, but laid-off workers, firms and borrowers lose.

items.prompt: Tulonga lends a neighbour N$10 000 at a fixed 6% a year in money terms. During the year of the loan, prices in the economy rise by 9%. Using the figures, explain who gains and who loses from the loan in real terms.
items.canonical_answer: Tulonga is repaid N$10 000 x 1.06 = N$10 600, but to keep up with 9% inflation she would need N$10 000 x 1.09 = N$10 900. The repayment buys less than the sum she lent, so her real return is negative, roughly 3% a year below zero. Tulonga, the lender, therefore loses in real terms. The neighbour gains, because the fixed money debt is repaid in money that buys less than when it was borrowed.

items.prompt: Define monetary policy and state how it is typically used against inflation.
items.canonical_answer: Monetary policy is the use of changes in interest rates, the money supply and the foreign exchange rate, usually by the central bank, to influence the economy. Against inflation it typically raises interest rates, so borrowing becomes dearer and spending grows more slowly.
marking_guidance: Precise definition: the meaning must be stated exactly - what the term is, and what it covers.

items.prompt: To slow a 6% yearly climb in prices driven by fast credit growth, the central bank raises its policy interest rate. Analyse the benefits of using an interest-rate rise to control inflation.
items.canonical_answer: The rate rise is aimed at the cause: prices are climbing on fast credit growth, and dearer borrowing slows exactly that, so total spending grows more slowly and the demand-pull pressure eases. It has wide reach, because commercial banks pass the higher rate on to loan and deposit rates across the whole economy, not one region or industry. It protects buying power: as the 6% climb slows, savers and households on fixed money incomes keep more of what their money buys. Consumers see prices climb more slowly, savers earn more on deposits, firms plan against steadier prices, and the government moves closer to its price stability aim.
marking_guidance: Benefit: each advantage must be stated as a benefit of the policy measure named.
Because: the reasoning must link the policy to its effect, so that the chain is written out.
For whom: the answer must say who gains - consumers, workers, savers, firms, the government or the economy.

items.prompt: Prices are rising because imported fuel has become dearer and firms are passing the cost on. Analyse the limitations of using higher interest rates to control this rise in prices.
items.canonical_answer: Higher rates miss the cause: this rise is cost-push, from dearer imported fuel, and dearer borrowing does nothing to the price of fuel, so firms face higher interest costs on top of higher fuel costs. The attempt is costly: dearer credit makes firms postpone expansion and households cut spending, so output grows more slowly and jobs weaken while prices stay pushed up. The effects also arrive months later, perhaps after the fuel price has moved on. Firms face dearer credit and weaker sales together, workers in loan-dependent industries carry the slowdown, consumers still pay the higher prices, and the economy gives up growth without reaching the cause.
marking_guidance: Limitation: each drawback must be stated as a limitation of the policy measure named.
Because: the reasoning must say why the drawback arises, so that the chain is written out.
For whom: the answer must say who bears the limitation - consumers, workers, borrowers, firms, the government or the economy.

items.prompt: Discuss whether raising interest rates is the most effective policy for a government to control inflation.
items.canonical_answer: Raising interest rates may be the most effective policy where prices rise on fast spending and credit, because dearer borrowing slows exactly that spending, banks pass the higher rate on across the whole economy, and a slower climb protects savers and fixed-income households. A low, steady rise in prices is easier to manage than the fast rise it prevents. It may not be, because it works on spending, not costs. Where fuel or harvests push costs up, dearer borrowing squeezes output and jobs without touching the cause, and its effect on spending takes months. It also slows growth and employment, whereas fiscal measures can be aimed more narrowly and supply-side measures can ease costs. On balance, a rate rise is the most effective single measure where the pressure comes from domestic spending and credit, as it is well aimed and economy-wide. It depends on the source of the rise: against demand-pull inflation it should lead; against cost-push inflation it is a costly side-measure while cost-side measures do the work.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer must reach a judgement, and it depends must be answered by naming the condition.
Why it might: the argument for must be developed with its mechanism.
Why it might not: the argument against must be developed with its mechanism.
Decisive: the answer must name what settles it - the condition the judgement depends on.

items.prompt: Prices in an economy have begun to fall and the central bank cuts its policy rate from 7% to 4%. A Katutura bakery is planning a N$150 000 oven on bank credit. Using the figures, explain how the cut is likely to affect the bakery's borrowing and the wider economy's spending.

Cheaper credit makes buying the oven now more worthwhile, so the bakery is likely to borrow and invest sooner, and households may borrow to spend too. However, where buyers expect prices to keep falling, they may still postpone purchases, so the cut supports spending but may not restart it quickly.

items.prompt: Facing a 6% yearly climb in prices driven by fast spending, a government cuts its own spending and raises taxes while the central bank holds interest rates. Analyse how this fiscal tightening is likely to work through the economy and whom it affects.
items.canonical_answer: When the government cuts its own spending and raises taxes, it buys less and households keep less income after tax, so total spending grows more slowly. Sellers can no longer count on buyers bidding against each other, so the demand-pull pressure eases and the 6% yearly rise in prices slows towards the price stability aim. But firms that sell to the government lose orders first, and output and jobs in those industries weaken while the tightening works. Taxpayers and users of public services bear the direct cost, those firms and their workers lose sales and hours, and consumers gain from prices climbing more slowly: a trade-off between the government's aims.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the range of policies available to control inflation.
items.canonical_answer: The three routes differ in who acts and what they work on. Monetary policy, run by the central bank, raises interest rates so borrowing is dearer and total spending grows more slowly. Fiscal policy, run by the government, cuts spending or raises taxes, and can be aimed at particular purchases or industries. Supply-side measures, such as training or cheaper transport, raise capacity or ease input costs, so they can reach cost-push inflation that spending restraint cannot. All serve price stability, and against deflation they run in reverse.
marking_guidance: Features: what it includes - each characteristic named and separated; a definition restated is not a features answer.

items.prompt: Define deflation.
items.canonical_answer: Deflation is a sustained fall in the general price level of an economy over a period, so that a unit of money buys more goods and services than before. A slower rise in prices is not deflation.
marking_guidance: Precise meaning: one mark for a sustained fall in the general price level, and one for the period or for money buying more than before. A slower rise in prices - from 4% to 2% a year, say - is not deflation, because the general price level is still rising, and a fall in one good's price is not deflation either.

items.prompt: An economy's Consumer Prices Index fell from 150.0 last year to 147.0 this year. Calculate the economy's yearly rate of change in the general price level.
items.canonical_answer: Rate = (CPI this year - CPI last year) / CPI last year x 100. 147.0 - 150.0 = -3.0; 3.0 / 150.0 = 0.02 and 0.02 x 100 = 2, so the rate is -2% a year: a 2% fall, so deflation.
marking_guidance: Formula: the yearly rate formula - (CPI this year - CPI last year) / CPI last year x 100 - must be stated or used, with last year's index as the base.
Substitution: the working shows the fall of 3.0 index points divided by 150.0, step by step.
Answer with units: -2% a year, a fall in the general price level, identified as deflation; a positive 2% is the wrong direction.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between a demand-side cause and a supply-side cause of deflation.
items.canonical_answer: The difference lies in what starts the fall. A demand-side cause is a fall in total spending - credit tightens or incomes drop - so firms cut prices to win the fewer buyers, and output and jobs tend to fall with prices. A supply-side cause is cheaper inputs or higher productivity, so firms can charge less without losing profit, and output can hold. The test is what happens to output: falling prices with falling output point to the demand side; falling prices with steady output point to the supply side.
marking_guidance: Boundary: the difference must be stated - a demand-side cause is a fall in total spending, whereas a supply-side cause is cheaper inputs or higher productivity - with the mechanism of each.
Test: the answer must give how to tell them apart - what happens to output and jobs as prices fall.

items.prompt: In one year prices in an economy rise by 10%, while the money wages of shop workers rise by 4%. A furniture maker finds its timber and fuel costs rising, and it raises its own prices by 8%. Using the figures, explain the consequences of this inflation for the shop workers and the furniture maker.
items.canonical_answer: Prices rose 10% but the shop workers' pay rose 4%, so their pay buys about 5.5% less, since 1.04 / 1.10 = 0.945: their real wage falls, and they are likely to press for higher pay. The furniture maker faces dearer timber and fuel and raises its own prices by 8%; whether it gains or loses depends on whether its costs rose faster than 8%. With prices rising this fast, the firm also finds costs harder to predict, so it may hold back investment.
marking_guidance: Context: the answer must use the figures - prices up 10%, shop workers' pay up 4%, the furniture maker's prices up 8%.
Reasoning: the link must be given - because pay rises more slowly than prices, the workers' real wage falls; because the firm's costs and prices both rise, its position depends on which rises faster.
Conclusion: therefore the workers lose buying power and may press for pay rises, while the firm faces uncertainty that may hold back investment.

items.prompt: Inflation in an economy rises unexpectedly to 12% a year, well above the 3% a year in its main trading partners. Analyse the consequences of this inflation for the economy as a whole.
items.canonical_answer: When prices rise 12% a year unexpectedly, costs and prices become hard to predict. Because firms cannot plan with confidence, investment tends to wait, so capacity grows more slowly. Workers press for pay rises to keep up, firms pass the higher wage costs on in prices, and costs climb again - a chase between prices and pay that keeps inflation high. Because domestic prices rise faster than the partners' 3%, exports become dearer against rivals' goods and imports relatively cheaper, so exporters may lose sales and the current account tends to weaken. Therefore growth, jobs in exporting firms and the external balance all tend to suffer.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - inflation rising unexpectedly to 12% a year against 3% in trading partners - must be named first.
Mechanism: because prices are hard to predict and run ahead of trading partners', this causes investment to wait, a chase between pay and prices, and a loss of export competitiveness.
Consequence: therefore growth, employment and the current account each need a traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - firms deciding on investment, workers, exporters and the economy as a whole.

items.prompt: Prices in an economy have fallen for two years, households expect further falls, and many factories stand idle. Discuss whether cutting interest rates and raising government spending are likely to end the deflation.
items.canonical_answer: The policies may work. Cutting rates makes borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding, so households and firms may bring spending forward; raising government spending adds orders directly, and with factories idle there is spare capacity, so the extra spending tends to raise output and jobs, lifting incomes and spending further and easing the pressure for prices to fall. They may not work quickly. Where households expect prices to keep falling, they may keep postponing purchases even when credit is cheap; if rates are already near zero, there is little room to cut; and higher spending adds to public borrowing that later taxpayers repay. Japan's long spell of falling prices persisted despite very low interest rates. On balance, the two together are more likely to succeed than either alone, because government spending adds orders even where borrowers hold back. What settles it is confidence: if households come to expect prices to stop falling, spending revives; if not, the policies work slowly.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the answer must reach a decision - on balance the combination is more likely to succeed than either policy alone - with its reason.
Why it might: the argument for - cheaper borrowing, direct orders from government spending, spare capacity letting output and jobs rise - developed to its consequence.
Why it might not: the argument against - expectations of further falls, little room to cut rates near zero, the burden of public borrowing - developed to its consequence.
Decisive condition: what settles it is confidence, whether households and firms stop expecting prices to fall.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. Inflation is best defined as:
A  a rise in the price of one good that many households buy
B  a sustained rise in the general price level over a period
C  a rise in the share of income a household spends on food
D  a fall in the quantity of goods a fixed sum of money buys, caused by cheaper imports

2. The Consumer Prices Index tracks:
A  the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services, weighted by spending shares
B  the price of the goods one household buys in one week
C  the total spending of the government in a year
D  the money wages of workers across the economy

3. The CPI rises from 128.0 to 134.4 in a year. The yearly rate of inflation is:
A  6.4%
B  5%
C  4%
D  0.05%

4. Demand-pull inflation arises when:
A  the costs of production climb and firms pass them on
B  the money supply shrinks and credit tightens
C  total spending grows faster than the economy's capacity to produce
D  a poor harvest pushes food prices up across the basket

5. Diesel becomes dearer and haulage firms pass the rise on to shop prices. This is:
A  cost-push inflation
B  demand-pull inflation
C  deflation caused by weaker demand
D  a rise in one price, leaving the general level unchanged

6. Which group tends to lose most in real terms from an unexpected rise in prices?
A  borrowers repaying fixed money debts
B  savers holding money and lenders repaid in fixed money sums
C  firms able to raise their own prices with costs
D  workers whose pay rises with prices at once

7. A household expects prices to keep falling and postpones buying a fridge. If many households act this way, the likely result is:
A  higher output as firms produce more
B  a self-feeding fall in spending, output and jobs
C  a rise in the general price level
D  no effect on firms, because needs return eventually

8. To slow a rise in prices driven by fast credit growth, the central bank is most likely to:
A  raise its policy interest rate
B  cut government spending directly
C  raise the weights of food in the basket
D  wait for input costs to fall on their own
items.canonical_answer:
Key: 1 B, 2 A, 3 B, 4 C, 5 A, 6 B, 7 B, 8 A.
1. B names the general level and the period (A confuses inflation with a single price, C with the weighting inside the index, D with a change in buying power read the wrong way round).
2. A names the fixed basket and the weights (B is one household's week rather than the typical household, C is fiscal, D is a labour market measure).
3. B divides the 6.4 point rise by 128.0 and scales by 100 (A states the point rise rather than the percentage, C mis-divides, D forgets the factor of 100).
4. C names spending outgrowing capacity (A describes cost-push, B describes a deflationary cause, D is a supply shock that pushes costs, not demand pulling).
5. A names the cost origin (B reverses the direction, C invents falling demand, D denies the spread to the general level that the passing-on causes).
6. B names the holders of fixed money claims (A gains from unexpected inflation, C passes the rise on, D keeps pace rather than losing).
7. B traces the postponement chain (A expects higher output from weaker sales, C reverses the direction of the price level, D ignores the fall in sales firms record meanwhile).
8. A is the monetary route aimed at credit (B is a fiscal tool the central bank does not hold, C confuses measurement with policy, D is waiting rather than acting).
marking_guidance: Key: one mark per question, eight in total; the correct option is listed and each distractor is explained as the specific misunderstanding it catches.

Each distractor traces to a named error: a single price read as the general level, a point rise read as a percentage, the causes of inflation swapped, the gainers and losers of inflation swapped, the postponement chain denied or reversed, the tools of the central bank and the government confused.

items.prompt:
An invented report, written for practice, in the Oshakati Times, 2026: "Prices rose faster this year than last, and shoppers at the open market say food is the reason. The statistics agency's index rose again in the twelve months to March, with food the leading item; clothing barely moved. The central bank has warned it may act, though the harvest, not credit, is what traders blame."

Table 1 - the economy, twelve months to March
  CPI, March last year: 128.0
  CPI, March this year: 134.4
  yearly rise in food prices: 9%
  yearly rise in transport fares: 6%
  yearly rise in clothing prices: 2%
  household A food share of spending: 60%
  household B food share of spending: 15%

(a) Calculate the economy's yearly rate of inflation between the two March readings. [1]
(b) State the yearly rise in food prices shown in Table 1. [1]
(c) Identify from Table 1 the two items whose prices rose more slowly than the CPI. [2]
(d) Explain why household A's cost of living is likely to have risen faster than the CPI. [4]
(e) Analyse what the data suggests about the economy in the twelve months to March. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) The rise is 134.4 - 128.0 = 6.4 index points. The rate is 6.4 / 128.0 = 0.05, and 0.05 x 100 = 5, so the yearly rate of inflation is 5%.
(b) Food prices rose 9% (from Table 1).
(c) Transport fares at 6% and clothing at 2% rose more slowly than the CPI's 5% (from Table 1).
(d) The CPI is an average weighted by spending shares, and household A's spending is concentrated on the fastest-rising item. Food alone contributes 0.60 x 9% = 5.4 percentage points to A's cost of living, already above the whole 5% rise in the index, so A's basket rises faster than the average. Because A spends a large share on food and food rose 9% while A's other purchases rose by less, the weighted average of A's own prices sits above the index. Therefore A's cost of living has risen faster than the CPI, where household B, spending 15% on food, faces a rise closer to the index or below it.
(e) A general price level rising 5%, led by one item - food at 9% against clothing at 2% - points to cost pressure from food reaching the whole basket rather than a broad spending boom, because the rise is concentrated where the harvest bit. The CPI moved from 128.0 to 134.4, a 5% rise; food rose 9% while transport rose 6% and clothing 2%, and households spending heavily on food - A at 60% - face more than the headline rate. A food-led rise of this shape tends to hit consumers on low incomes hardest, since food takes the largest share of their spending, so the buying power of their incomes falls fastest even while the index reads 5%. If workers then win higher wages to keep up with food prices and firms pass those wage costs on, the rise could spread across the basket - a further cost-push route. The central bank's warning would fit demand-pull pressure, but the data shows nothing about credit rising. However, clothing at 2% shows the rise is not equally strong across the economy, and household B, at a 15% food share, faces a cost of living rising by less than the index - the average hides both directions at once.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) and (b) are 1 mark each, read or calculated from Table 1; (c) is 2 marks, 1 per item; (d) is 4 marks, one per distinct linked statement; (e) is 6 marks.
Context: (d) and (e) must use the figures - the 128.0 to 134.4 index move, the 9% / 6% / 2% item rises, and the 60% and 15% food shares.
Reasoning: one mark per distinct linked statement; quoting a figure from Table 1 on its own is evidence, not analysis - a figure without the linked statement it supports earns nothing in (e).
Conclusion: (e) must run expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception, and name for whom the effects land.

facts: CPI 128.0 last March and 134.4 this March
food prices rose 9%, transport fares 6%, clothing 2%
household A spends 60% of its income on food, household B 15%

items.prompt:
An economy's prices have risen 6% a year for two years, driven first by fast credit growth and lately by dearer imported fuel.
(a) Define inflation. [2]
(b) Explain the difference between demand-pull inflation and cost-push inflation. [4]
(c) Analyse the consequences of a period of falling prices for consumers, firms and workers. [6]
(d) Discuss whether the government should use higher interest rates to deal with the economy's fast rise in prices. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level of an economy over a period, usually a year, so that a unit of money buys fewer goods and services than before.
(b) The difference lies in what rises first. Demand-pull inflation begins on the spending side: total spending in the economy grows faster than its capacity to produce, buyers compete for scarce goods, and prices are pulled up by that competition - fast credit growth pulling prices up is the demand-pull case. Cost-push inflation begins on the cost side: the costs of production rise - dearer imported fuel is the cost-push case - and firms pass the rise on in higher prices with total spending unchanged. The test that tells them apart: ask what changed first. Where spending ran ahead first, the inflation is demand-pull; where costs rose first and prices followed, it is cost-push - and the economy here shows both in sequence, so the answer to which policy fits turns on which cause is doing the work at the time.
(c) When the general price level falls and buyers come to expect further falls, they postpone purchases they can put off, so firms' sales fall; firms cut prices again to win the buyers there are, cut output, and lay off workers. Workers who lose income spend less, prices fall further, and the fall can feed itself into a lasting drop in spending and output. At the same time each debt fixed in money becomes heavier in real terms, because each unit of money now buys more, so households and firms cut spending further to service their debts. Consumers who keep their incomes gain cheaper goods, but by postponing together they weaken the markets they buy from; firms face falling sales and margins; workers carry the lay-offs and shorter hours; and borrowers find the real weight of their debts rising as the price level falls.
(d) Higher interest rates suit the first cause of this economy's rise in prices - fast credit growth - because dearer borrowing slows exactly the spending that pulled prices up, and the higher rate reaches the whole banking system at once, protecting the buying power of savers and fixed-income households as the rise slows; a low, steady rise in prices is easier for an economy to manage than the fast rise the policy prevents. Against this, the latest pressure is cost-push - dearer imported fuel - and dearer borrowing does nothing to the price of fuel, so the measure risks squeezing output and jobs while prices stay pushed up by costs; the effects arrive with a delay, so a rise announced now may land after the fuel price has moved on; and the policy trades against the government's other aims, slowing growth and employment while it works. On balance the government should use higher interest rates while credit growth is the main driver of the rise, because the instrument is aimed at that cause and reaches the whole economy. The judgement depends on the source of the pressure at the time: whether prices are being pulled up by spending or pushed up by costs. Where fuel is doing the work, measures on the cost side bear the burden better and at lower cost in jobs.
marking_guidance: Parts: (a) 2 marks for two creditable elements of the definition; (b) 4 marks, one per distinct linked statement; (c) 6 marks, one per distinct linked statement with its reason carried; (d) 8 marks, level-marked over three bands.

Bands for (d): Level 3 (top) examines why it might and why it might not, then reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on - the source of the price pressure; Level 2 develops one side or asserts a judgement without the condition; Level 1 offers fragments of either side.
For whom: (c) must name the consumer, the firm, the worker and the borrower at each step, and (d) must land its costs and returns on named parties.
Context: (b) and (d) must use the economy's own sequence - credit growth first, imported fuel lately.

facts: prices rose 6% a year for two years
first cause fast credit growth, latest cause dearer imported fuel

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "Discuss whether deflation is a more serious problem for an economy than inflation." Build the plan from the causes and consequences of each. Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for (deflation is the more serious):
Point 1: deflation chains into output. Chain: prices fall and buyers expect further falls -> purchases are postponed -> firms cut output and lay off workers -> the workers' lost income cuts spending again, a self-feeding spiral inflation does not match (who is affected: workers lose posts; firms lose sales; the economy loses output).
Point 2: deflation raises the real burden of debt. Chain: the price level falls while debts stay fixed in money -> each unit of money buys more, so more goods must be given up to service each loan -> households and firms cut spending to keep paying -> spending falls and the fall deepens (who is affected: borrowers carry more; lenders are repaid in money worth more, so the burden shifts against debtors).
Case against (inflation is serious too):
Point 1: inflation redistributes and scrambles planning. Chain: prices rise faster than expected -> savers and lenders on fixed money sums lose buying power, borrowers gain -> firms cannot predict costs, wage bargaining turns into a chase -> investment waits and exports lose ground where domestic prices outrun rivals' (who is affected: savers, lenders, fixed-income households lose; firms plan less; the economy invests less).
Point 2: the seriousness depends on the cause of the deflation. Chain: where falling prices come from cheaper inputs and higher productivity -> firms charge less without losing profit -> the price level falls while output holds (who is affected: consumers gain cheaper goods with no loss of jobs) - so supply-side deflation of this kind is less damaging than a fast inflation.
Judgement: deflation is the more serious problem where it is demand-side - driven by weak spending and feeding itself - because policy struggles to restart spending once buyers wait, whereas inflation driven by spending can be slowed with interest rates and does less harm while it is moderate. The condition the judgement depends on is the cause and speed of each: a mild supply-side fall in prices may be benign, and a fast inflation is worse than a gentle fall - so it depends on which economy, which cause, and how fast.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the case for, the case against, each point as a chain, and the judgement with the condition it depends on.
Each chain states its starting point, its mechanism and the consequence for a named party - consumers, workers, borrowers, savers, lenders, firms or the economy.
The judgement must settle on the condition: the cause of the deflation and the speed of each price movement, since a supply-side fall is a different problem from a demand-side spiral.
